facts.statement: The genus Feilongus was named and described in 2005 by Wang Xiaolin, Alexander Kellner, Zhou Zhonghe, and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
facts.quote: The genus was named and described in 2005 by Wang Xiaolin, Alexander Kellner, Zhou Zhonghe and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

facts.statement: The specific name youngi honors the Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian.
facts.quote: The specific name honors the Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian (C. C. Young).

facts.statement: The type specimen is holotype IVPP V-12539, a crushed skull and articulated mandible of a subadult individual.
facts.quote: Feilongus is based on holotype IVPP V-12539, a skull and articulated mandible, with on the same plate the detached posterior braincase, of a subadult individual.

facts.statement: A second specimen, DNMHM D3068, found at Gonggao in 2014, was referred to Feilongus.
facts.quote: In 2014, a second specimen, DNMHM D3068 found at Gonggao, was referred to a Feilongus sp.

facts.statement: Feilongus lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous in the Yixian Formation of Beipiao, Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Feilongus is an extinct genus of ctenochasmatid pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Barremian–Aptian-age Lower Cretaceous Yixian Formation of Beipiao, Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: Feilongus lived between 125.77 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Feilongus had an estimated wingspan of 2.4 meters (7.9 feet), which is large for a basal pterodactyloid.
facts.quote: The wingspan of Feilongus was estimated by Wang and colleagues to have been around 2.4 meters (7.9 feet), making it large for a basal pterodactyloid.

facts.statement: The holotype skull of Feilongus is 390–400 millimeters long, extremely elongated with a slightly concave top.
facts.quote: The skull of the holotype is 390–400 millimeters long (15.4–15.7 inches) and extremely elongated with a slightly concave top.

facts.statement: Feilongus had 76 long, curved, needle-like teeth confined to the anterior third of its jaws.
facts.quote: The skull and lower jaws held 76 long, curved needle-like teeth, eighteen in the upper, nineteen in the lower jaw, confined to the beak ends, the anterior third, of the jaws.

facts.statement: The neck vertebrae of the second Feilongus specimen are very elongated, being five times longer than wide.
facts.quote: The neck vertebrae of the second specimen are very elongated, five times longer than wide.

facts.statement: A 2018 phylogenetic analysis places Feilongus as a ctenochasmatid in the subfamily Moganopterinae with its sister taxon Moganopterus.
facts.quote: A 2018 phylogenetic analysis recovers Feilongus as a ctenochasmatid. Specifically, Feilongus is placed with its sister taxon Moganopterus in the subfamily Moganopterinae:

facts.statement: It is debated whether Feilongus is an archaeopterodactyloid or a member of the Ornithocheiroidea closer to the Anhangueridae, based on a 2006 analysis by Lü Junchang.
facts.quote: However, in 2006 an analysis by Lü Junchang had as outcome that Feilongus was not an archaeopterodactyloid, but a member of the Ornithocheiroidea sensu Kellner, closer to the Anhangueridae.

facts.statement: Some researchers have proposed placing Feilongus and Boreopterus in a new family called Boreopteridae.
facts.quote: Another publication following this general line of thought has put Feilongus and Boreopterus into a new ornithocheiroid family, the Boreopteridae.

facts.statement: Ctenochasmatoids like Feilongus are hypothesized to have used their numerous small, thin teeth to strain food from water, similar to flamingos.
facts.quote: The Ctenochasmatoidea are known for having numerous small, thin teeth, possibly for straining food from water, as flamingos do today.

facts.statement: If Feilongus is classified within the Ornithocheiroidea sensu Unwin, its members are typically adapted for soaring and a fish-eating diet.
facts.quote: a group the members of which are typically more adapted to soaring and a piscivore, or fish-eating, diet.

rejected.quote: The genus name is derived from Feilong, the 'flying dragon'.
